title: Home Anniversary Ideas & Text Templates for Realtors
summary: Home anniversary ideas for realtors by budget and by year, plus text templates for first-time buyers, downsizers, investors and clients who moved away.
body_markdown:
Your clients get birthday messages from their dentist and their bank. Nobody else remembers the day they got their keys.


That's why the home anniversary is the best touch in a past-client plan. It starts from a memory you share, and it hands you a reason to get in touch every year without making one up. NAR's 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers puts the typical seller's time in their home at 11 years, so a client you close with this year may not move again until the late 2030s. You'll get a lot of anniversaries out of one client.


This guide covers what to send, what it should cost, how to make each year useful instead of repetitive, and text templates for the clients a generic message doesn't fit. If you want the full calendar these sit inside, see our[12-month plan for staying in touch with past clients](https://getdex.com/blog/how-to-stay-in-touch-with-past-clients/) .


**Fast facts:**


-


Typical seller tenure is 11 years, per NAR's 2025 profile, so plan for a decade of anniversaries per client.


-


A text costs nothing and is the easiest thing to reply to. Save gifts for your top 20 to 30 clients.


-


The IRS lets you deduct business gifts up to $25 per person per year. Anything above that is on you.


-


Year one is when most seller-paid home warranties run out, which is a genuinely useful reminder to send.


-


PMI must drop off automatically when the loan is scheduled to hit 78% of the original value, per the CFPB. Clients rarely know this.


*Image: A past-client record in Dex, with the close date and notes from the deal*


## Why the anniversary works better than any holiday card


Holiday cards arrive in a pile with forty others. An anniversary message arrives alone, on a date that means something to the client, and it opens with a memory you both have. That's why it gets replies.


It also scales gently. If you've closed 150 deals, your anniversaries are spread across the year at about three a week. That's a few minutes a week, and every one of them is a real conversation instead of a broadcast.


The trap is sending the same "Happy home anniversary!" every year. By year three, the client can tell it's automated. The fix is to give each year its own reason.


## Make each year useful


Below is a year-by-year guide. Send the text either way. Adding the useful thing turns a greeting into a small favor.


Anniversary


Useful thing to mention


Why it matters to them


Year 1


Their home warranty is probably about to expire


Most seller-paid warranties last a year. Renewing or getting the HVAC checked before it lapses can save a repair bill.


Year 2


Property tax assessment and homestead status


The first full reassessment often lands now. If the number looks wrong, many counties have an appeal window.


Year 3


Whether they've built enough equity to drop PMI


Borrowers can ask to cancel PMI at 80% of the original value. Prices may have moved them there early.


Year 5


What homes on their street have sold for


Five years is when equity gets interesting. Share real numbers, not a pitch.


Year 7


Bigger maintenance (roof, water heater, exterior paint)


Original systems start to age. A trusted vendor list is worth more than a gift.


Year 10 and up


A life-stage question: still the right fit?


Kids leaving, aging parents, retirement. Don't push a sale. Ask how the house is working for them.


A couple of cautions. Check tax deadlines with your county, because they vary a lot. On PMI, the CFPB says servicers must end it automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value, and borrowers can request it at 80%. FHA and VA loans have their own rules. You're pointing them toward a question for their lender, not giving loan advice.

On taxes: the IRS caps the deduction for business gifts at $25 per recipient per year, per Publication 463. A $100 print is still a nice gift. Just know that only $25 of it counts as a business expense. If you're thanking someone for a specific referral, that's a separate question with state rules of its own. Our guide on[asking past clients for referrals](https://getdex.com/blog/how-to-ask-past-clients-for-referrals/) covers it.


Pop-bys deserve a word. They're the most memorable thing on this list and the most expensive in time. Twenty pop-bys can eat a Saturday. Do them for people who will genuinely enjoy seeing you, and leave a note if nobody's home instead of making a second trip.


## Text templates


Keep anniversary texts short and specific. The memory is what makes it land. Fill the brackets from your notes, and if you don't have a detail, use the street name and a question.


**First-time buyers, year one:**


"Happy one year, \[Name\]! I still think about how nervous you were signing that first page. How does it feel to be a homeowner a year in? Also, heads up: your home warranty probably runs out around now if you want to renew or get the AC serviced first."


**Move-up buyers:**


"One year at \[street\] today! Has the extra bedroom turned into an office or a playroom? Hope it's been everything you wanted."


**Downsizers:**


"A year since you moved into \[street\]. I hope the smaller place has given you back a lot of weekends. How are you liking it?"


**Investors:**


"Three years since we closed on \[address\]. Happy to pull current rents and sales on that block if it would help with your planning."


**Sellers who moved out of your area:**


"It's been a year since you handed over the keys on \[street\]! How's life in \[new city\]? If anyone back here ever needs an agent, I'd love to help them."


**Clients you helped through a hard sale (divorce, estate, relocation):**


"Thinking of you today, a year since we closed. I hope this year has been a good one. No need to reply, just wanted you to know I remembered."


Leave out "happy" and the confetti emoji on that last one. For a sale that came out of a death or a divorce, the anniversary may not be a happy date. Your notes from the deal will tell you which clients these are.


**Year five, with real numbers:**


"Five years at \[street\] today! Fun fact: the last three sales on your block averaged about \[number\]. Not a hint, just thought you'd like to know. Hope you're still loving it."


**Year ten:**


"Ten years in your home today. That's a big one. How's the house working for you these days? Same as ever, or are things changing?"


Year ten is a good place for a real call instead of a text if you have the time.

## Keeping track of a few hundred close dates


The hard part of anniversaries isn't writing the message. It's knowing that today is the day for the Hendersons, and remembering that the Hendersons almost lost the house over the sewer scope.


You need two things on every past client's record: the close date and one or two details from the deal. A spreadsheet holds the dates. It won't tap you on the shoulder, and it gets clumsy when you want the story next to the name.

## Who this isn't for


If most of your business is investors flipping or renting, an annual anniversary text is fine but it's not your main touch. Investors care about deals, so a monthly note on what's coming up will do more.


And if you've got 40 past clients, you don't need a system. Put the dates in your phone's calendar with a one-line note and you're done.


## FAQ


### What do you send a client for their home anniversary?


A short, personal text that mentions something from their deal is enough for most clients. Save gifts, cards and pop-bys for your top 20 to 30 clients and anyone who has referred you.


### What should a home anniversary text say?


Name the year, mention a specific memory or detail about the house, and ask a question so they reply. For example: "One year at Maple Street today! Did the basement ever flood like you were worried it would?"


### How much should a realtor spend on a home anniversary gift?


Nothing for most clients, and around $25 for your best ones. The IRS only lets you deduct $25 per person per year in business gifts, so more expensive gifts come out of your own pocket.


### Should I send home anniversary messages every year?


Yes, but change the reason each year so it doesn't feel automated. Year one can mention the home warranty, year three can be about PMI, year five can share sales on their street.


### Is a home anniversary card better than a text?


A text costs nothing and is easier to reply to, so it's the better default. A handwritten card stands out once in a while, especially for year one or year ten.


### Should I ask for a referral in a home anniversary message?


Not in the first message. If the client replies warmly, that's a good moment to mention that you'd love to help anyone they know. Asking every year turns the anniversary into an ad.


## The bottom line


Every client gives you one free, personal reason to reach out every year. Send a short text that remembers something, add one thing that's useful for the year they're in, and keep the gifts for the people who send you business. Keep it up for a decade and you'll be hard to forget when they finally move.
